explanations: luna: The section contrasts useless sparks with a lamp or morning light; this parable has people kindle a fire, briefly see by its light, then have their light taken away and remain in darkness. | terra: A kindled fire briefly lights its surroundings before God takes the light and leaves darkness; it is the clearest Quranic boundary between momentary ignition and enduring illumination.
terra: Lightning gives just enough intermittent light to walk before darkness makes people stop, a natural parallel to the instant spark that cannot become the section's lasting morning.

luna: In the section a stone is struck to make fire; here stones are named among the fire’s fuel, reversing their role from fire-making tool to what is consumed. | terra: In the warned-of Fire, people and stones are fuel; stone here sustains fire by being consumed rather than serving as the struck tool from which a spark escapes.

luna: The section describes a hard strike on stone releasing sparks; here Moses strikes a stone by God’s command and water springs out, a specific reversal in what a blow on stone releases. | terra: A commanded strike on stone makes twelve springs burst out; the same hard contact with stone yields water rather than the fire produced in the section's striking scene.
terra: Stones are described as bursting or splitting so that water emerges from them; the same hard object releases the opposite element from the section's spark-producing stone.
terra: Wealth cannot benefit its owners against God and they become fuel for the Fire, tightly joining prized possessions, failed benefit, and fire.

luna: The section links the fire-name نار الحباحب to 100:8’s حُبّ الخير; this verse names “الخيل المسومة” among the worldly desires people love, placing the horse scene beside wealth and attachment. | terra: The love of desires is adorned through gold, silver, and marked horses among other possessions, directly joining the ح ب ب family, prized wealth, and horses in one ayah.
terra: Consultation over the matter, followed by resolve and trust, gives a positive Quranic form of the source dictionary's figurative striking of an affair through examination and planning.

terra: The different ء ن س usage فَإِنْ آنَسْتُمْ مِنْهُمْ رُشْدًا means perceiving sound judgment in orphans; it links perception to the image's question of whether human thought finds guidance or error.
terra: Skins consumed by fire are replaced so that punishment is tasted anew, a concrete Quranic instance of fire transforming the surface it touches.
luna: Moses hopes to find “هدى” at the fire in 20:10; here God guides by His light and brings people from darkness to light, distinguishing true direction from the section’s spark of misguidance.

luna: The section says a person can try to strike the flint of misguidance; here people kindle “نارا للحرب” and God extinguishes it, a specific destructive fire whose intended force is cut off. | terra: Whenever opponents kindle a fire for war, God extinguishes it; this is a direct reversal of the source dictionary's reviving of a dormant fire and of ignition that succeeds.

luna: The section’s dictionary form الصباح means daylight and its prose says morning replaces darkness; here God is “فالق الإصباح” and makes night for rest, directly placing dawn against night. | terra: God is فَالِقُ الْإِصْبَاحِ and appoints night for rest; the same ص ب ح family presents dawn as a divinely opened boundary after darkness.
terra: One brought from death to life is given a light by which to walk among people, while another remains in darkness; resurrection, guidance, and useful illumination meet without a literal flame.

luna: This retelling likewise has Moses strike a stone, but twelve springs flow from it; it gives a second Quranic outcome for the stone-strike scene, water rather than the section’s sparks. | terra: The repeated Moses account again has a staff strike stone and water issue in twelve springs, a precise elemental reversal of striking stone for sparks.
terra: People destined for Hell have hearts with which they do not understand, repeating the precise link between failed human reason and fire stated in 67:10.
terra: Hoarding gold and silver and withholding them establishes the attachment for which the next ayah heats that treasure and brands its owners.
terra: Hoarded gold and silver are heated in Hell and used to brand bodies, joining love of wealth to the source's sense of fire scorching or branding what it touches.
terra: A human construction founded at a crumbling brink collapses with its builder into Hellfire, giving the section's successful-versus-wasted undertaking question a material and fiery form.
terra: Lot is told that morning is his people's appointed time of destruction—“is morning not near?”—so the ص ب ح boundary brings judgment rather than simply secure daylight.
terra: People in the Fire have exhaling and inhaling; this places breath inside the fire scene, echoing the section's linkage of dabh-breath with heat and ash.

luna: This describes material heated “في النار” for adornment or use, then distinguishes foam that vanishes from what benefits people and stays; it develops the section’s contrast between useless airborne sparks or ash and lasting benefit. | terra: Metal is heated in fire, useless scum rises, and what benefits people remains; the verse gives the image's fleeting spark versus useful result a precise material analogue.

luna: The section’s dictionary branch calls the remains of fire “الرماد”; here rejecters’ deeds are compared to ash scattered by storm wind, extending the physical residue into an image of effort with no lasting gain. | terra: The deeds of rejecters become ashes driven violently by wind, making the source dictionary's dabh-as-ash into an image of an effort from which nothing can be retained.

luna: The section mentions the burning brand “شهاب قبس”; this ayah’s “شهاب مبين” follows one who steals a hearing, a Quranic use of the same flame-word for a directed act rather than useless sparks. | terra: A clear flaming projectile pursues anyone who steals a hearing; the airborne شِهَاب repeats the useful firebrand word of 27:7 in a hostile celestial function.
terra: The blast seizes the people of Lot in the morning, repeating the ص ب ح boundary as the arrival of destruction rather than benign illumination.

luna: The section sets a brief spark against morning light that lets people see; this verse says the night’s sign was effaced and the day’s made visible so people can see and seek provision. | terra: God erases the sign of night and makes the sign of day visible so people can seek bounty and reckon time, giving durable daylight the usefulness the section's instant sparks lack.
terra: “Be stones or iron” names the two materials of the section's fire-making tool inside a challenge about resurrection, joining its physical apparatus to the same proof made with fire in 36:80.
terra: Whenever Hell subsides, God increases its blaze, a dark eschatological counterpart to the source dictionary's act of stirring a fading fire back into flame.
terra: The guilty see the Fire and know they will fall into it with no escape, opposing Moses's hopeful sight of a distant fire that yields news and guidance.

luna: The section’s fire-making tool is iron struck against stone; here iron is worked until it is heated like fire and molten metal is poured over it. The link is the iron-and-fire craft, though this ayah builds a barrier rather than making a spark. | terra: Iron blocks are blown upon until they become fire-hot, then covered with molten metal; iron, force, heat, and a useful finished work recast the section's physical ignition scene.
terra: The question about the greatest losers in deeds opens a Quranic counterpart to the section's choice between an undertaking that catches and a spark spent in vain.
terra: Their effort goes astray in worldly life while they think they are doing well, precisely rendering a mind that strikes the “flint of misguidance.”
terra: God's call to Moses from the right side of the Mount and drawing him near recount the same revelatory encounter as the distant-fire narratives without repeating the fire detail.

luna: The section’s root ء ن س appears in “إني آنست نارا”; Moses hopes either for a firebrand or “هدى” there, making the distant fire a possible practical aid and guide. | terra: Moses's إِنِّي آنَسْتُ نَارًا leads him to seek a firebrand or guidance at the fire, realizing both the source's ء ن س sense and its question of what a spark will become.

luna: This is the next moment after Moses reaches the fire in 20:10: he is called by name, and the hoped-for sign becomes an address. | terra: When Moses reaches the fire he is called by name, the first concrete fulfilment of the guidance he hoped to find in 20:10.

luna: The call at the fire continues with an instruction to remove his sandals because he is in the sacred valley; it locates the guidance Moses hoped to find. | terra: The voice at the fire tells Moses to remove his sandals because he is in the sacred valley Tuwa, identifying the fire-site as holy rather than merely a place to collect an ember.

luna: The same encounter tells Moses he has been chosen and must listen to revelation, giving concrete content to the “هدى” sought at the fire in 20:10. | terra: After the call at the fire, God chooses Moses and commands him to listen to revelation, specifying the guidance that 20:10 only anticipated.

luna: The call identifies Allah and commands worship and prayer for remembrance; this is the guidance that follows Moses’ search at the fire. | terra: The guidance found at the fire becomes recognition of God, worship, and remembrance, giving the distant light a durable human consequence.

luna: The fire encounter’s speech continues from the guidance Moses seeks in 20:10: this ayah says the Hour is coming and each soul is recompensed for its striving, meeting the section’s dictionary sense of a kindled undertaking reaching its aim.

luna: The same speech warns Moses not to be turned aside by someone who rejects the Hour and follows desire; it gives a specific form of the section’s contrast between a purposeful spark and the spark of misguidance.
terra: Moses burns the calf and then scatters it into the sea, a complete Quranic movement from burning an object to dispersing what remains.
luna: The section presents fire as an ignition whose output may be useful or futile; here God commands the fire to be cool and safe for Abraham, a specific reversal of fire’s ordinary burning effect.

luna: The section contrasts fleeting sparks with a lamp and lasting daylight; this parable describes a “مصباح” whose oil nearly shines before fire touches it and says God guides to His light, a useful light unlike the sparks “لا ينتفع به.” | terra: The source dictionary's مِصْبَاح appears in a niche, fueled by a blessed tree whose oil nearly shines without fire; sustained lamp-light answers the image's futile airborne sparks.
terra: Lightning from the clouds nearly snatches sight, another Quranic flash whose intense but momentary light differs from the stable light of morning and lamp.

terra: Moses sees a fire from far away and approaches it; here the Fire itself sees its people from a distant place and they hear its rage, reversing observer and observed as well as hoped-for benefit.
terra: Night is a covering, sleep a rest, and day a rising again; the replacement of darkness by day becomes an image of resurrection, joining both major claims developed around the spark.
luna: The section names مصباح and its dictionary form سراج; this verse places a “سراجا” in the sky beside an illuminating moon, giving the lamp image a heavenly counterpart to a short-lived spark.
terra: God's call commissioning Moses to go to the wrongdoing people states the mission that comes out of the revelatory encounter first approached as a useful fire.

luna: The section cites Moses saying “إني آنست نارا” and “بخبر”; this telling adds the possibility of a “بشهاب قبس,” joining the root of seeing a fire to the root خ ب ر named at the surah’s end. | terra: Moses says إِنِّي آنَسْتُ نَارًا and expects خَبَر or a شِهَابٍ قَبَسٍ; the seen flame joins the source's ء ن س sense, a portable ember, and the خ ب ر family of 100:11.

luna: After Moses comes to the fire he is called and the place is blessed; the expected news or ember leads directly into divine address. | terra: Arrival at the fire yields a divine call, blessing, and glorification, showing that this distant flame gives far more than physical warmth or a passing spark.

luna: This gives the content of the call begun at the fire: Moses is told that the speaker is Allah, the Mighty and Wise, fulfilling the search for guidance with a source. | terra: The caller at the fire identifies Himself as God, the Mighty and Wise, supplying the authoritative news for which Moses approached.
terra: The queen refuses to decide her affair before counsel is present, another concrete instance of carefully “striking” a matter in the source dictionary's figurative sense.

luna: The section links 100:6’s root ء ن س to seeing a fire and 100:11’s root خ ب ر to news; Moses says “إني آنست نارا” and hopes to bring “بخبر,” joining both links in one scene. | terra: Moses يَسْتَأْنِسُ a fire from the side of the mount and approaches for خَبَر or a firebrand, staging the source's ء ن س sense while linking the promised news to 100:11's خَبِير.

luna: This continues the fire scene from 28:29: when Moses reaches it, a call comes from the blessed place by the tree, turning his search for news into an encounter with revelation. | terra: On reaching the fire, Moses is called from a tree in the blessed place; the neighbour supplies both the news promised in 28:29 and a striking meeting of fire and tree.
terra: The addressee is reminded that he was not beside the Mount when God called; this retrospective reference confirms the fire journey as a revelatory scene transmitted as mercy.
luna: The section contrasts a brief spark with morning light; this asks who could bring light if God made the night continuous, directly marking the dependence of people in darkness on real light.
luna: The paired question asks who could bring night for rest if God made day continuous; it sets the section’s morning light within the reciprocal night-and-day boundary.
terra: God brings the living from the dead and the dead from the living and revives earth after death; this states the reversal made tangible when fire issues from a green tree.
terra: After Satan has led multitudes astray, the rebuke “did you not reason?” gives the section's “flint of misguidance” an explicit Quranic formulation.
terra: Hell is then identified as the promised destination, connecting the failure of reason in 36:62 to fire.
terra: The misled are commanded to burn there because of their rejection, completing the sequence from failed reasoning to destructive fire.

luna: This opens the passage about the question the section cites in 36:78: a human is reminded that God created him from a drop before he disputes how decayed bones can live again, grounding the dispute in first creation. | terra: The human being forgets creation from a drop and becomes an open disputant, establishing why the bone question and fire answer are needed.

luna: The section identifies this challenge about “من يحيي العظام وهي رميم”; it makes the fire that follows an answer to a human limit placed on resurrection. | terra: The objection asks who can revive decayed bones, the precise resurrection denial to which the green-tree fire of 36:80 responds.

luna: This answers the bone question named in the section: the one who first brought them into being can revive them, preparing the fire example in 36:80. | terra: The answer points to the One who originated the bones the first time, stating the resurrection inference that the following fire-from-tree image makes perceptible.

luna: The section explicitly uses this answer: God made fire from the green tree, and people “منه توقدون”; familiar ignition becomes evidence of the Creator’s power to revive. | terra: Fire issuing from a green tree joins apparent opposites, and the surrounding resurrection argument turns ordinary kindling into evidence that life can issue from death.
terra: Creation of the heavens and earth is invoked as the larger measure of God's ability to recreate humans, continuing the inference begun with fire from green wood.
terra: God's command “Be” explains how re-creation follows from the power illustrated by fire issuing from green wood.
terra: The resurrection proof closes by glorifying the One in whose hand is dominion and to whom all return, paralleling the doxological close of the fire sequence in 56:74.

luna: The section mentions Moses’ “شهاب قبس” and sparks flying in air; here a “شهاب ثاقب” pursues a listener in the heavens, turning a similar aerial flame into a purposeful guard. | terra: A piercing شِهَاب pursues the one who snatches a hearing; the fiery object named as a useful carried ember in 27:7 becomes an airborne projectile.
terra: The warned are told how evil their morning will be when punishment descends, making صباح carry the opposite valence from the section's lasting morning light.
terra: Fine standing horses are displayed to Solomon at evening, supplying the horse scene in which the next ayah's exact “love of good” wording occurs.
terra: Solomon says that he loved the love of good while responding to the horses; حُبَّ الْخَيْرِ brings the runners and the exact love-of-good expression of 100:8 together outside surah 100.
terra: Those who listen to speech and follow its best are the guided people of understanding, a positive counterpart to striking the source dictionary's “flint of misguidance.”

luna: The section defines مصباح through the dictionary form سراج; this verse says the lowest heaven is adorned with “مصابيح” and guarded, giving the Quranic lamp a protective, enduring role unlike useless sparks in the air. | terra: The lowest heaven is adorned بِمَصَابِيحَ, using the source dictionary's lamp word for fixed celestial lights rather than sparks that vanish in the air.
terra: A settled punishment reaches Lot's people at morning; the same ص ب ح moment that displaces darkness in the section here makes the coming consequence endure.

terra: The passage's skeptics ask whether death, dust, and bones can really be followed by resurrection; that is the objection addressed by the crop, water, and fire questions culminating in 56:71–73.
terra: “We created you; why do you not affirm?” introduces the divine agency that the following crop, water, and fire questions unfold against resurrection denial.
terra: Remembering the first creation is offered as the inference the deniers should draw before the passage proceeds through seed, water, and fire.

luna: The section explicitly says the resurrection passage asks about crops as well as fire; this opens the paired question about what people cultivate, placing human use of provision beside the fire they kindle. | terra: The first أَفَرَأَيْتُمْ question turns to what people till, opening the crop-water-fire sequence cited by the section.

luna: This is the crop question the section names: people sow, but God asks whether they make it grow or He does, paralleling the distinction between kindling fire and creating its source. | terra: The contrast between human sowing and God's causing growth establishes the same hidden agency later asked about the fire's tree.

luna: In the crop passage the section identifies, God says He could make the harvest dry debris; the possible loss of what people cultivate extends the section’s concern with fire’s ash and what remains. | terra: God could reduce the crop to broken debris; within the sequence this supplies a non-fire analogue to the source's progression from heat to residue.

luna: This continues the crop question named by the section: the people’s response to a ruined harvest shows their dependence on provision rather than authorship of it. | terra: After the imagined crop is crushed, people recognize themselves as burdened by loss, registering the failure of what had seemed a successful human undertaking.

luna: The crop passage continues with the people saying they have been deprived; this is their response to the loss whose possibility 56:65 establishes, within the provision sequence the section names. | terra: The further admission that they are deprived makes explicit that useful provision was never secured by human effort alone.

luna: The section explicitly names the water question that precedes its fire question; this begins the parallel challenge about the source of a daily provision. | terra: The second أَفَرَأَيْتُمْ question turns to the water people drink, the middle member of the crop-water-fire proof named in the section.

luna: This continues the water question the section names, asking whether people send down what they drink or God does; it parallels the distinction between using a provision and creating it. | terra: As with the fire's tree, the verse asks whether people brought the water down or God did, exposing provision behind apparent human use.

luna: The water sequence the section names ends with God’s power to make it bitter and a question about gratitude, preparing the same recognition of divine provision that surrounds the fire question. | terra: God could make the water bitter; this counterfactual clarifies that usefulness is bestowed, preparing for the useful fire of 56:73.

luna: The section names 100:2’s root و ر ي and notes the same fire-making verb in “النار التي تورون”: God asks people to consider the fire they kindle, distinguishing the act of striking it from creating its source. | terra: The exact و ر ي root of the source's مُورِيَات returns in the question about the fire تُورُونَ, the fire people make emerge.

luna: The section points to fire made from a tree; this neighboring question asks whether people created “شجرتها” or God did, sharpening the gap between kindling and originating the material. | terra: The question whether people created the fire's tree or God locates the source behind the apparently human act of kindling.

luna: This completes the fire passage the section cites: God made it “تذكرة ومتاعا” for travelers, giving a useful, reminding purpose against the horses’ sparks that “لا ينتفع به.” | terra: God makes that fire both a reminder and a practical provision; this directly answers the section's distinction between a useful fire and the horse-spark that benefits no one.

luna: After the section’s cited fire is called a reminder and provision in 56:73, this neighboring ayah commands glorifying the Lord; it supplies the worshipful response to the created fire’s reminder. | terra: The fire proof concludes with a command to glorify the name of the Supreme Lord, fixing the stance the preceding questions are meant to produce.
terra: Hypocrites ask believers to wait so that they may نَقْتَبِسْ from their light, but no share is available; the sought qabas reverses Moses's successful quest for a firebrand and guidance.
terra: Iron is sent down with great strength and benefits for people; the metal used as the section's striking tool is here explicitly measured by durable human benefit.

luna: As in 2:24, the section’s stone that starts a flame is reversed here: the fire’s fuel includes stones, making the same object part of what burns. | terra: The Fire guarded by angels likewise has people and stones as fuel, turning the section's human use of stone for ignition into an eschatological reversal.
terra: On Judgment Day believers' light runs before them and they ask God to complete it, an enduring eschatological light set against sparks that do not illuminate.

luna: The section calls sparks flying through the air useless; this ayah names the sky’s “مصابيح” and says they are made as missiles against devils, a specific contrast between airborne fire that has no use and lights given a purpose. | terra: Celestial مَصَابِيح adorn the sky and also serve as missiles, combining lasting lamps with moving fiery projectiles in one image.
terra: Hell is heard شَهِيقًا as it boils, making breath and raging fire coincide just as the section hears heat and ash within the runners' breath.
terra: The people of the Blaze admit that listening or reasoning would have kept them from it, directly joining misuse of the mind to a fire that is the outcome of that failure.
luna: The section’s dictionary form سراج for مصباح appears here for the sun, while the moon is called “نورا”; the steady heavenly lights set the lamp image against momentary sparks.
luna: This opens the passage about the heavens being filled with guards and flames, the setting for the next ayah’s waiting “شهابا”; it broadens the section’s airborne-fire image to guarded skies.

luna: Continuing 72:8, this says a listener now finds a “شهابا رصدا”; alongside the section’s “شهاب قبس” and useless flying sparks, it depicts an airborne flame with a specific purpose. | terra: A listener now finds a flaming projectile lying in wait, another concrete airborne شِهَاب set against Moses's portable ember and the horses' harmless sparks.
terra: The man فَكَّرَ وَقَدَّرَ, thinking and calculating before a disastrous judgment, directly enacts the source dictionary's figurative “striking” of a matter by examining and planning it.
terra: ثُمَّ نَظَرَ continues the deliberate looking named in the source dictionary, while its place in the sequence shows that scrutiny alone does not ensure a sound result.
terra: After thinking and looking, the man turns away in arrogance; this ayah marks the decisive misuse of the deliberation whose false verdict follows.
terra: The man's deliberation produces the false verdict that revelation is transmitted magic, the failed intellectual “spark” anticipated by the section.
terra: Calling revelation merely human speech completes the wrong conclusion reached after thought and inspection.
terra: The response “I will burn him in Saqar” joins the preceding corrupt deliberation to the fire later described as scorching skin.
terra: Saqar neither leaves nor spares, setting total consumption against the source's account of fire leaving ash behind.

luna: The section’s dictionary branch says sun or fire can change an object’s color; “لواحة للبشر” is commonly read as Saqar scorching or blackening human skin, though the word has interpretive range, giving a destructive counterpart to that color-changing branch. | terra: Saqar is لَوَّاحَةٌ لِلْبَشَرِ, scorching or blackening human skin; this is the Quranic counterpart to the source's fire that changes a thing's colour.

luna: The section says the spark flashes briefly in darkness before morning takes its place; this oath marks the night as it departs, the dark side of that boundary. | terra: The retreating night supplies the darkness-side of the transition completed by the oath to morning in 74:34.

luna: The paired oath names “والصبح إذا أسفر,” morning as it brightens; it directly matches the section’s image of daylight displacing darkness after a brief spark. | terra: وَالصُّبْحِ إِذَا أَسْفَرَ depicts morning unveiling its light, a direct ص ب ح formulation of the image's durable replacement of darkness.

luna: This fire throws “بشرر كالقصر”; its deliberately immense sparks give a Quranic counterpart to the section’s sparks made when stones collide, while the surrounding passage describes punishment rather than useful ignition. | terra: Hell throws out شَرَرٍ, sparks, giving a direct Quranic scene of fire scattering sparks through the air.

luna: This continues the sparks of 77:32, comparing them to yellow camels; it completes the fire’s vivid image without making the sparks useful. | terra: The preceding sparks are compared to yellow camels, extending the airborne-spark scene while unexpectedly returning it to an animal form.
luna: The section gives سراج as a dictionary form for مصباح; the Quran calls the blazing heavenly lamp “سراجا وهاجا,” a sustained radiance unlike the fire’s airborne sparks.
terra: The Lord calls Moses in the sacred valley Tuwa, another direct formulation of the encounter reached by following the fire in 20:10–13.
terra: Hell is set ablaze at the final upheaval, placing ignition itself inside the resurrection horizon that the section reaches through ordinary kindling.

luna: The section contrasts a fleeting spark with morning’s light; “والليل إذا عسعس” marks the night at the boundary, but عسعس is used both for night drawing on and retreating, so only the retreating sense sharpens the contrast with 81:18. | terra: The withdrawing night is the immediate counterpart to morning's breathing in 81:18 and completes that light-over-darkness scene.

luna: The section’s dictionary sense of الصباح is daylight; “والصبح إذا تنفس” presents morning as arriving after the night, a direct boundary between darkness and enduring light. | terra: وَالصُّبْحِ إِذَا تَنَفَّسَ makes morning itself breathe, bringing the first ayah's breath and the third ayah's dawn together as darkness gives way.
terra: The trench contains a fire full of fuel, foregrounding the prepared combustible material required for a spark to become sustained flame.
luna: The section develops morning as daylight that displaces darkness; this oath names “الفجر,” dawn itself, another direct Quranic formulation of the light-boundary image.

luna: The section’s wordplay joins the sparks called الحباحب to حُبّ الخير; this verse makes love of wealth “حبا جما,” clarifying the intense attachment in that same word-family without itself describing fire. | terra: وَتُحِبُّونَ الْمَالَ حُبًّا جَمًّا repeats the surah's love-of-wealth sense of ح ب ب, the same family in which the source finds the useless horse-spark's name.
luna: The section contrasts a momentary spark with the day’s light; this oath names the day “إذا جلاها,” when it reveals, as the bright counterpart to the covering night in 91:4.
luna: This paired oath says “والليل إذا يغشاها,” the night as it covers; it gives the darkness from which the section’s spark flashes and morning emerges.
luna: The section’s spark appears against darkness and yields to day; this oath names the night “إذا يغشى,” the covering phase of the boundary with 92:2.
luna: This paired oath names “والنهار إذا تجلى,” the day as it appears; it echoes the section’s daylight that replaces darkness rather than flickering briefly.
terra: A person's wealth will not benefit him when he falls, restating the image's question of whether prized gain becomes any lasting or useful result.
terra: The warning of a blazing fire supplies the fiery outcome of the nearby miser's self-sufficiency and wealth that cannot benefit him.

luna: The section connects 100:8’s intense love of “good” with worldly wealth; this ayah describes the wealth-collector who amasses and counts it, giving a concrete form to that attachment before the fire passage in 104:6-7. | terra: Collecting and repeatedly counting wealth supplies the human project whose imagined gain ends in the kindled fire of 104:6.
terra: The wealth-counter thinks his property has made him last forever, directly opposing the section's question of what momentary effort can truly endure.

luna: The section ties an unhelpful horse-spark to the neighboring love of wealth; in the passage about the wealth-collector, this is “نار الله الموقدة,” a kindled fire with real consequence rather than a spark that benefits no one. | terra: نَارُ اللَّهِ الْمُوقَدَةُ is a deliberately kindled fire, and its placement after wealth-counting makes fire the end of a human project that was mistaken for lasting gain.

luna: This continues 104:6 by saying the kindled fire rises over hearts; next to the section’s wealth-love and useless “hubabib” sparks, it gives that fire-word a consequential, inward counterpart. | terra: The kindled fire rises over hearts, turning the fire image inward toward the human interior and the motives behind wealth-love.
terra: Abu Lahab's wealth and gains do not benefit him, restating in personal form the section's pairing of coveted good with something ultimately useless.
terra: He enters a fire of flame immediately after his wealth is declared useless, making the wealth–nonbenefit–fire sequence explicit.
terra: Seeking refuge in the Lord of daybreak presents dawn as an opening cut through darkness, a nonlexical parallel to the section's morning that replaces the spark-lit night.
